explanations.explanation: That's the one, baker. Jesus says, “Whoever believes in Me, as the Scripture has said: ‘Streams of living water will flow from within him.’…” The water doesn't come from a spot on a map or a checklist. It flows from the person who believes in Him, and it flows from the inside.

I get why this one is tempting, friend. Plenty of folks figure the best-behaved person gets the prize. But Jesus never says that here. He says, “Whoever believes in Me…” and then the streams of living water flow from within him (John 7:38). Believing is the whole invitation, and I'm glad, because my perfect-behavior record has a few crumbs on it.

A place name is an easy pick, so I see how you got here. But Jesus never ties the water to an address. He says, “Whoever believes in Me…” and then the streams of living water flow from within him (John 7:38).

Right on the money, baker. The Gospel of John tells us straight out, “He was speaking about the Spirit, whom those who believed in Him were later to receive.” So the living water is about the Spirit. And John doesn't leave us guessing, which I appreciate, because I've followed recipes with less help than that.

The law was a big topic in that crowd, so I see the pull. But John explains the living water himself, and he doesn't say law. He says, “He was speaking about the Spirit, whom those who believed in Him were later to receive.” The Gospel gives us the answer right there in the verse.

The temple sounds like a natural pick, friend, so I see the pull. But the writer doesn't say the water is about the temple. He says Jesus “…was speaking about the Spirit, whom those who believed in Him were later to receive.” When the writer hands you the answer, take it and say thank you.

That's it, baker. Some say, “This is truly the Prophet.” and others declare, “This is the Christ.” (John 7:40-41). Same speech, different conclusions. One invitation and the crowd is already splitting into batches.
I see why Elijah popped into your head, friend. But the text doesn't record anyone in this crowd saying that name. What it records is others declaring, “This is the Christ.” (John 7:41).
Jeremiah is a good name to know, baker. But the text doesn't record anyone saying it here. It says some called Jesus the Prophet, and others declared, “This is the Christ.” (John 7:40-41).

Yes, baker. These folks ask, “How can the Christ come from Galilee?” (John 7:41). They're saying Galilee doesn't fit what they expect. And they've got Scripture on their minds when they ask it, which I respect.

Samaria is a real place in that part of the world, so I see the guess. But it's not the one the crowd names. They ask, “How can the Christ come from Galilee?” (John 7:41). Galilee is the place they're stuck on.

Egypt shows up all over the Bible, so I'll give you credit for a big swing. But this crowd isn't talking about Egypt. The question is, “How can the Christ come from Galilee?” (John 7:41). It's Galilee that has them scratching their heads.

Yes, baker. The text says, “So there was division in the crowd because of Jesus.” (John 7:43). Some said Prophet, some said Christ, and some had questions. Same words, same moment, and the crowd split every which way.

I can see why you'd hesitate, friend, but this one is true. John says plainly, “So there was division in the crowd because of Jesus.” (John 7:43). Some called Him the Prophet, some called Him the Christ, and some asked about Galilee. The crowd did not agree.

I get why you'd say that, because some of them did want to grab Him. But the text goes on: “Some of them wanted to seize Him, but no one laid a hand on Him.” (John 7:44). So the answer is False. Wanting to and doing it turned out to be two very different things.

That's right, baker. John says, “Some of them wanted to seize Him, but no one laid a hand on Him.” (John 7:44). The wanting was there, but nobody followed through. That's some folks wanting to grab the dough and never getting a hand on it.

explanations.answer: Never has anyone spoken like this man
explanations.explanation: That's the one, baker. The officers answer, “Never has anyone spoken like this man!” (John 7:46). Remember, they were sent to bring Jesus in (John 7:32). And they came back with that answer instead of Him.

explanations.answer: Never has anyone drawn a crowd like this
explanations.explanation: Crowds are an easy guess, so I get it. But the officers don't say a word about crowds. They say, “Never has anyone spoken like this man!” (John 7:46). Their answer is about His words.

explanations.answer: Never has anyone stood up to us like this
explanations.explanation: That sounds like something a worried boss might expect to hear, friend. But the officers don't say it. They answer, “Never has anyone spoken like this man!” (John 7:46). It's about the way He spoke, not about standing up to anyone.

I see why you'd think the bosses would nod along, baker, but they don't. The Pharisees reply, “Have you also been deceived?” (John 7:47). So the answer is False. They answer the officers with a question of their own, and it isn't agreement.
Correct, baker. The Pharisees don't agree. They reply, “Have you also been deceived?” (John 7:47). Instead of agreeing, they ask the officers if they've been fooled.
Yes, baker. The Pharisees say, “But this crowd that does not know the law—they are under a curse.” (John 7:49). Curse is the word the text gives them. You picked it right out of the batch.

Blessing is a word people like to hear, friend, so I see the pull. But that's not what the Pharisees say. The text has them saying, “But this crowd that does not know the law—they are under a curse.” (John 7:49).

A vow is a real thing in the Bible, so I see why it came to mind. But that's not the word here. The Pharisees say the crowd that doesn't know the law is “…under a curse.” (John 7:49). Curse is the word the text gives.

explanations.answer: Whether it convicts a man before hearing him
explanations.explanation: That's it, baker. Nicodemus asks, “Does our law convict a man without first hearing from him to determine what he has done?” (John 7:51). He's asking about their own law, in front of the group he belongs to. I think that took guts.

explanations.answer: Whether it lets officers arrest at a feast
explanations.explanation: The officers did come back without Jesus, so I see how your mind went there. But Nicodemus asks something else. He asks, “Does our law convict a man without first hearing from him to determine what he has done?” (John 7:51). His question is about hearing a man out first.

explanations.answer: Whether it allows healing on the Sabbath
explanations.explanation: Healing on the Sabbath is a fair guess, friend. But it's not what Nicodemus asks here. He asks, “Does our law convict a man without first hearing from him to determine what he has done?” (John 7:51). His question is about hearing a man before judging him.
Yes, baker. They answer him, “Aren’t you also from Galilee?” (John 7:52). They don't answer his question about the law at all. They turn it right back around on him.

I can see why this might sound off, friend, but it's true. They answer Nicodemus with, “Aren’t you also from Galilee?” (John 7:52). Nicodemus asked about their law, and they answered with a question about where he's from.
